lesson.menu_title: Arrivals — The First Two Hours in a Country You Do Not Know
lesson.menu_desc: A missed connection, a closed border and the two hours that decide the whole trip -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Arrivals
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 10 -- Arrivals

listenings.text: Ladies and gentlemen, this is an announcement for passengers travelling on the delayed service to Istanbul. Regrettably this flight will not now depart this evening. The border has closed to overflights and our crew have reached the end of their permitted hours. Hotel accommodation will be provided and vouchers are being distributed at the gate. Please note that rebooking cannot be carried out at this gate. Passengers with onward connections should proceed to the transfer desk in the arrivals hall, which is on the level below, and which will remain open. Passengers without onward connections should remain here. We are extremely sorry for the disruption to your journey this evening, and we will make a further announcement within the hour.

I have worked nights on a transfer desk for eleven years, so let me tell you what actually works, because it is not what people think. The single most useful thing you can do is ask a question I am able to answer. When will the flight go? I do not know, nobody in this building knows, and asking me twelve times will not change that. Can you rebook me tonight, on any airline, to anywhere within two hundred kilometres of my destination? That I can work with. Second thing. Shouting fails, and not for the reason people assume. It is not that we take offence. It is that the person you are shouting at usually has no authority to change anything, and the person who does have that authority is standing behind them deciding who to help first. And third, and I mean this quite literally: we remember the calm ones. At three in the morning, being remembered is worth a great deal.

extra_audio.text: Yasmin says it is her third night this month in a terminal and that her system is mostly about not being angry. He answers that the hardest part for him is the pointlessness of the waiting. She explains that she leaves the queue and looks for the one person with information. He asks how she finds that person at three in the morning. She answers that specific questions find specific people, and describes the question she asks.

paras: Every trip has two hours that decide how the rest of it feels, and they are never the two hours in the photographs. They begin the moment the aircraft door opens and they end when you have somewhere to sleep and some idea of where you are. Handled badly, they colour everything that follows. Handled well, they are invisible.

The mechanics are always the same. Having landed, you queue. Not knowing the layout, you follow the person in front, who does not know it either. Immigration takes between four minutes and two hours and there is no way to predict which. Given a delay of any size, your onward travel is now a question rather than a plan, and the desk that could answer it closes at eleven.

What separates travellers is not experience but the first decision after that. The inexperienced ones optimise: they look for the cheapest transfer, the fastest route, the best rate, at two in the morning, having slept for three hours on a red-eye. The experienced ones do the opposite. They take the first safe option at any price, get to a bed, and make every real decision the following morning, having got their bearings and eaten something.

There is one more thing, and it is the reason this is a language lesson and not a travel column. In those two hours you will speak to five or six people, all of them tired, none of them interested in you, several of them speaking English as a second language exactly like you. Faced with that, most people go silent and point. The ones who do not — who ask a clear question, take the answer in their stride and ask a second one — arrive somewhere entirely different, and it has almost nothing to do with vocabulary.
